# The pinned libghostty-vt archives

`nocx` links ghostty's `libghostty-vt` statically — it is the terminal emulator
the session runtime is built on (ADR-0065). This directory is how that
dependency is held: **one manifest of pins**, **one recipe that rebuilds every
archive from them**, and **one fetch that verifies before a build links
anything**.

The owner's decision, 2026-09-13 (`nocx-ygxjv.10`):

> pinned, identical results; prebuilt archives preferred over building
> everywhere, because a verified file gives identical bytes by construction
> while a from-source build on a pinned toolchain gives identical source and
> only hopes for identical bytes.

## Layout

| path                             | what it is                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `MANIFEST.json`                  | the pin: the fork commit and the upstream one it patches, Zig, build flags, and per target the sha256 of the archive and its headers |
| `licenses/`                      | licence texts committed for the two components whose pinned inputs ship none, each with its origin                                   |
| `stubs/`                         | two empty `.tbd` files that let a Linux host cross-link a darwin binary (see `stubs/README.md`)                                      |
| `scripts/recipe.sh`              | rebuilds every archive and the licences document from the pin, then verifies them                                                    |
| `scripts/licenses.sh`            | generates `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES` from the pin and the archives that were built from it                                               |
| `scripts/verify-link.sh`         | proves every archive LINKS — and that the Linux ones link statically — with a probe that calls it                                    |
| `scripts/measure-helper-size.sh` | what `make helpers` produces per target, for the size budget                                                                         |
| `scripts/stage-notices.sh`       | stages the pinned `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES` where a binary can carry it: the helper's embed directory, the macOS bundle, the AppImage   |
| `linkprobe/`                     | the probe itself: a nested Go module, not a binding (the binding is `internal/emulator/ghostty`)                                     |

Nothing generated by any of this lives in the tree, with **one exception, and it
is a constraint rather than a choice**: the helper's copy of the licences
document is staged into `internal/helper/notices/licenses/`, because a
`//go:embed` cannot escape the package directory it is written in — the same
limit `internal/transport/ws_notify.go` states for the contract bounds it cannot
read. That staged file is a copy of the document `build/libghostty-vt/` holds
and carries no second verification of its own; it is gitignored, and its
directory carries a committed `.gitignore` so a checkout that has never fetched
the pin still compiles.

Everything else the pin produces stays out of the tree: the source checkout and
Zig's caches go to `~/.cache/nocx/libghostty-vt`, fetched and built archives go
to `build/libghostty-vt/` (gitignored, and already ignored by eslint and
prettier). That is deliberate rather than tidy: a ghostty source checkout inside
the repository breaks the root eslint run, because ghostty's own tree contains
JavaScript (found committing `nocx-ygxjv.7`). No ignore rule is added for it —
the checkout is simply never there.

## The fork, the patch, and what a release carries

**The source is a FORK of ghostty, `shady2k/ghostty`, at a commit that carries
nocx's patches.** `MANIFEST.json` records all four facts a reader needs to see
that: the fork's `repository`, the `commit` the archives were built from, the
`baseCommit` that commit sits on, and a one-line `patch` describing the
difference — `Validate` refuses a commit that differs from its base without
saying what the patch is, and refuses a `patch` on an unpatched pin. The tag the
fork carries at the base is `nocx-pin-e2e53f861482`; the archives are built from
the branch on top of it.

**There is no source tarball asset any more** (`nocx-ygxjv.14`). ADR-0065 point 1
asks for a controlled copy of the source rather than a SHA on somebody else's
host, and the fork's git history at that commit IS the controlled copy — in the
same repository the archives are published from. A 39 MB tarball beside it would
be a copy of a copy, and the one artifact nobody builds from.

**The release carries the licences too.** Every binary that links the archives
statically links ghostty, Highway, Wuffs, uucode, simdutf and Zig's
`compiler_rt`, so `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES` — generated from the archives
themselves, not from a list somebody maintains — is a pinned asset like any
other. See "Third-party licences" below.

## Six archives, four targets, and why not fewer

A static archive's libc is baked into its objects. Built naively for
`x86_64-linux` (glibc) and linked into a Go program, the result is **dynamic** —
`PT_INTERP` plus `libc.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `librt.so.1`; the same code
against the `-musl` build is **0 and 0**. The helper that runs on an unknown
remote host must be the second kind. The ordinary native build —
`go build -tags gtk3 ./...`, `go test -race`, CI's Linux jobs — is glibc. So
both exist, and neither is a fallback for the other. The pair is a statement
about the host a binary is FOR, not a workaround for a link that fails: measured
on 2026-09-13 while wiring the adapter (`nocx-ygxjv.2`), each archive does still
link under the other's compiler — what the choice fixes is which libc the linked
objects were built against, and `make helpers` is what makes it, with `-tags
vtmusl` for its Linux targets:

| target            | Zig triple           | libc   | who links it                                  |
| ----------------- | -------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `linux-amd64`     | `x86_64-linux-musl`  | musl   | the shipped helper (`make helpers`)           |
| `linux-arm64`     | `aarch64-linux-musl` | musl   | the shipped helper                            |
| `linux-amd64-gnu` | `x86_64-linux`       | glibc  | native Linux builds: `make test`, CI, `-race` |
| `linux-arm64-gnu` | `aarch64-linux`      | glibc  | the same, on arm64                            |
| `darwin-amd64`    | `x86_64-macos`       | system | the helper and the app on macOS               |
| `darwin-arm64`    | `aarch64-macos`      | system | the same                                      |

**Do not set a musl C compiler repository-wide.** Zig is the helper's compiler
(`make helpers` asks `vtfetch cc --target <goos/goarch>` for it, per target) and
nowhere else. On macOS the static property was never held anyway: the darwin
helper this repository has always shipped already carries `LC_LOAD_DYLIB` for
`libSystem` and `libresolv`, because Go's own darwin runtime links them
(measured, `nocx-cm1ac`).

## Where a build finds them

`vtfetch fetch` materialises exactly the layout the CGo link files name:

```
build/libghostty-vt/vendor/<target>/libghostty-vt.a
build/libghostty-vt/vendor/<target>/include/ghostty/vt.h
build/libghostty-vt/vendor/<target>/include/ghostty/vt/*.h
```

so a link file inside the repo reaches its archive by resolving `${SRCDIR}` —
three directories up from `internal/emulator/ghostty/` — and choosing the target
by build constraint. The adapter's own lines in
`internal/emulator/ghostty/terminal.go` are the authority; this is their shape:

```go
#cgo linux,amd64,!vtmusl CFLAGS: -I${SRCDIR}/../../../build/libghostty-vt/vendor/linux-amd64-gnu/include
#cgo linux,amd64,!vtmusl LDFLAGS: ${SRCDIR}/../../../build/libghostty-vt/vendor/linux-amd64-gnu/libghostty-vt.a -lm -lpthread
#cgo linux,amd64,vtmusl CFLAGS: -I${SRCDIR}/../../../build/libghostty-vt/vendor/linux-amd64/include
#cgo linux,amd64,vtmusl LDFLAGS: ${SRCDIR}/../../../build/libghostty-vt/vendor/linux-amd64/libghostty-vt.a -lm -lpthread
```

`vtmusl` is what selects the musl pair, and glibc is deliberately the untagged
default so the many ordinary builds here get the archive their compiler is
configured for. `linkprobe/` spells the same PATHS with the opposite tag — its
`!gnu` files are the musl probe and its `gnu` files the glibc one — because a
probe is built BOTH ways by `scripts/verify-link.sh`, while the adapter is built
once per target.

The directory is under `build/` because git, eslint and prettier
already ignore it: a downloaded artifact is build output, and teaching three
walkers about a fourth directory is how a directory ends up in a commit.

## Using it

```bash
make vt-archives                     # fetch + verify (a build's first step)
make helpers                         # the four helper targets, archives linked
make vt-verify-link                  # every pinned archive links; Linux pair is static
make vt-helper-size                  # the sizes the size budget is derived from
make vt-recipe-audit                 # rebuild from the pin and report the diff
make vt-recipe-pin                   # rebuild and RECORD the result as the pin
```

`make helpers` needs the pinned Zig — 0.16.0, the version ghostty's
`build.zig.zon` declares — on `PATH` or in `$ZIG`. `vtfetch zig` checks the
version and refuses a different one rather than building bytes nobody pinned.

`make helpers` also needs the archives, which come from the FORK's GitHub
release — the one `release.assetURLTemplate` names. **That release must exist
before this lands**: it is published out of band by the coordinator, and the
product release workflow only ever _fetches_ from it — a release pipeline that
had to publish the archives it builds with would be circular. For a pre-publish
run, or to test a fetch without network, point it at a local directory:

```bash
make vt-archives VT_ASSETS=build/libghostty-vt/dist
```

For a pin whose commit is not pushed yet — the coordinator builds a fork
branch's archives before publishing that branch — point the recipe at the
checkout. It checks the checkout is AT the manifest's commit, so it can be a
different tree on disk but never a different revision of one:

```bash
make vt-recipe-pin VT_SOURCE=build/ghostty-fork
```

## The script surface

`cmd/vtfetch` is the only reader of `MANIFEST.json` — the Makefile, CI and these
scripts never re-parse it, so a field cannot mean two things:

| command         | what it does                                                        |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fetch`         | verify, and download what is missing, into `--root`                 |
| `plan` / `meta` | the target table (TSV) / the scalar pins (`key=value`) for scripts  |
| `pin`           | record the hashes of `--dist` into the manifest (a new pin)         |
| `verify`        | check `--dist` against the manifest, without writing                |
| `pack-headers`  | pack a headers directory into a deterministic bundle                |
| `licenses`      | generate `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES` from the pin and the built archives |
| `cc`            | print the C compiler for one target (`--libc musl\|glibc\|system`)  |
| `zig`           | resolve the pinned Zig, refuse a different version                  |
| `inspect`       | linkage and symbols of built files (`--require-static`, `--symbol`) |

The fetch is stateless and self-verifying: a file already on disk is re-hashed
against the manifest and left alone when it matches, and a file that does not
match is downloaded to a temporary neighbour, verified, and renamed — so a
tampered or substituted archive stops the build instead of linking into it, and
a failure never damages the artifacts already verified.

## Reproducibility, stated exactly

The archives are the identity guarantee: they are files, the release carries
them, and `vtfetch fetch` refuses any byte that is not the sha256 this manifest
pins. That is by construction and needs no toolchain.

`scripts/recipe.sh` is the other half — it rebuilds all six archives from the
pin and runs `vtfetch verify`. **A rebuild does not reproduce the archives**,
and that was measured rather than assumed, on 2026-09-13:

- Two builds of `linux-amd64-gnu` from the **same build root, same Zig binary,
  same flags** produced archives of exactly the same size (18,413,024 bytes)
  that differ in **60 bytes**. The second build of a pair is reproducible — the
  same state twice gives the same hash — so it is the _cache state_, not
  randomness, that moves it.
- Those 60 bytes are **Zig's own cache directory names**, embedded in the
  objects: `.zig-cache/o/bf349a4b…/libghostty-vt-static_zcu.o/` from a warm
  cache against `.zig-cache/o/3a6fad02…/…` from a cold one, and the same for
  `src/ghostty/.zig-cache/o/<key>`. Nothing about source, toolchain or flags
  determines those keys, so no pin can fix them.
- Earlier runs, from different build roots, differed the same way plus by
  size — 18,412,152 against 18,412,958 bytes for linux/amd64 — with 53
  embedded occurrences of the build root and 68 of Zig's installation
  (`lib/zig/std`, `libcxx`, `libc` headers).

**What does reproduce byte for byte, in every run above: the header bundles and
the licences document.** The bundles are built by `pack-headers`, whose
timestamps, owners, order and gzip header are fixed in code; the document is
generated from the source at the pin rather than compiled, so nothing about a
build can move it.

So read the recipe's output rather than its exit code: it is an **audit** that
names exactly which files are not the pinned bytes, and a mismatch is the norm
for the archives. This is the owner's reason for shipping archives instead of
building everywhere, stated in the decision this directory implements — a
verified file gives identical bytes by construction, while a from-source build
on a pinned toolchain gives identical source and only hopes for identical bytes.
It does not get the hope.

`MANIFEST.json` records the builder in one field, `build.canonicalHost`
("linux/amd64, Zig 0.16.0"), because that is evidence about the files a
publisher uploaded. It deliberately records **no paths**: a pinned pathnames a
configuration under which the bytes still differ, which would read as a
reproduction recipe while being none. The script prints the paths a run
actually used, so a diff is attributable without a field that cannot be
honoured.

Ghostty's own Zig dependencies are addressed by content hash in the pinned
`build.zig.zon` and fetched by Zig itself, so source + toolchain is the whole
input set — it just is not a whole answer to "the same bytes".

## Bumping the pin

```bash
# 1. edit MANIFEST.json: upstream.commit / baseCommit / patch, toolchain.zig,
#    release.tag (derived from the commit), and the URL template if the release
#    name changed
# 2. rebuild and record what was built (the archives you will publish), from
#    the fork commit — add VT_SOURCE=<checkout> if it is not pushed yet
make vt-recipe-pin
npx prettier --write third_party/libghostty-vt/MANIFEST.json
# 3. prove the recorded bytes link, on every target
make vt-verify-link
# 4. read the diff, then publish build/libghostty-vt/dist/ (see below)
```

Re-running `make vt-recipe-audit` afterwards will report the archives as
mismatched, because a rebuild does not reproduce them (see "Reproducibility").
That is the tool working: the manifest pins the FILES, and the files are what
the release carries.

## Publishing

Not done by this repository's automation, and not by a task brief: uploading a
release is an outward-facing act. Once `scripts/recipe.sh` has produced
`build/libghostty-vt/dist/`, it is one command, and nothing in the code needs
editing afterwards because the fetch's URL and hashes both come from the
committed manifest. It goes to the FORK, whose tag that manifest names:

```bash
gh release create --repo shady2k/ghostty libghostty-vt-6ea3d0e55a00 \
  --title "libghostty-vt @ 6ea3d0e55a00" \
  --notes "Pinned archives built from ghostty e2e53f861482 + nocx's DECRQM patch, plus the licences of what they link (ADR-0065). Fetched and verified by cmd/vtfetch; see third_party/libghostty-vt/MANIFEST.json." \
  build/libghostty-vt/dist/*
```

**There is no `--prerelease` any more, and that is a consequence of the fork
rather than a relaxation.** The flag existed because the archives used to be
published as a release of `nocx` itself, whose `releases/latest/download` the
updater resolves (`internal/update`, `updater.go:175`), and GitHub's `latest`
skips prereleases. The fork is not a repository the updater looks at, so the
flag guarded nothing; `release.prerelease` is gone from the manifest with it
(`nocx-ygxjv.14`).

## Third-party licences

Every binary that links these archives statically links the components inside
them, so it owes their licences: ghostty (MIT), Highway (Apache-2.0 OR
BSD-3-Clause), Wuffs (MIT OR Apache-2.0), uucode (MIT), simdutf (MIT OR
Apache-2.0, plus a BSD-3 notice embedded in its isadetection code) and Zig's
`compiler_rt` (MIT).

`THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES` is GENERATED — by `scripts/licenses.sh`, which drives
`vtfetch licenses` — from two places, and neither is a list somebody keeps:

- **The archives say which components.** `internal/vtpin` reads each archive's
  object members and the `zig-pkg/<directory>` paths those objects embed, and
  attributes them with rules whose measurement is written beside each one
  (`internal/vtpin/components.go`). A member no rule covers is an ERROR — that
  is a dependency linked without a licence — and so is a dependency directory no
  entry claims.
- **The source at the pin holds the texts.** A dependency's own licence files
  come out of its `zig-pkg` directory; ghostty's from the source root.

Two components ship NO licence file in the pinned inputs at all: simdutf is
vendored as an amalgamation whose wrapper copies no licence, and a Zig
installation carries no `LICENSE` for the `compiler_rt.o` it contributes. Their
texts are therefore committed under `licenses/`, and every entry in the
document's `ORIGIN` line names the upstream file the copy came from, its
version, and its sha256 — a licence text with no stated origin is worse than
none, because it looks checkable and is not.

`internal/vtpin`'s coverage test is what makes this more than prose: it reads
the pinned archives and the pinned document and fails if any component either
side knows about is missing from the other, in both directions. It needs
`make vt-archives` to have run — every CI job that compiles a CGo package
fetches the pin first — and it says so rather than skipping.

### Where the notices travel

Which binaries owe them, today, is one command: `go list -deps ./cmd/nocx-helper`
reaches `internal/emulator/ghostty`, and `go list -deps .` and
`go list -deps ./cmd/nocx-server` do not — the runtime ADR-0065 decided lives in
the helper. What a release ships is still a bundle carrying that helper, so the
document travels with both.

Generating the document is half of it; the licences have to reach the binaries,
which is a packaging question and has one owner:
`scripts/stage-notices.sh <destination>` resolves the asset name and its sha256
through `cmd/vtfetch` (the manifest's only reader), copies
`build/libghostty-vt/<asset>` — the document the fetch verified — to the
destination the caller names, and refuses bytes that are not the pin's. Three
destinations, one per thing a user downloads:

- **The helper**, embedded through `internal/helper/notices` and printed by
  `nocx-helper --licenses`. Embedded rather than deployed as a sibling file,
  because D7's install is content-addressed on the BINARY: the directory key is
  the sha256 of the decompressed helper and `.install-complete` claims every
  byte of it is durable, so a second file in that directory is bytes the claim
  does not cover. The artifact naming is frozen too — `source.go` derives a
  platform from `nocx-helper-<goos>-<goarch>.gz`, so a sibling named in that
  family parses as a platform that does not exist. One installed file carries
  its own licences, and the document is 61,163 bytes: the linux/amd64 helper
  measures 17,125,496 bytes against 17,064,248 for the same build with the embed
  directory empty, so the notices cost 61,248 bytes — the text plus the embed
  table and alignment, about 0.4% of the binary.
- **The macOS bundle**, `Contents/Resources/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt`, staged
  before `codesign` seals the tree; the release job re-hashes the file out of the
  bundle afterwards. A bundle is what a user receives and it ships the helper
  that links the archives, so the document travels in it rather than only inside
  the binaries — a reader who never runs `--licenses` still has the licence texts
  beside the app.
- **The Linux AppImage**, `usr/share/doc/nocx/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt`; the
  packaging script extracts the file back out of the finished artefact and
  hashes it against the pin there, so an AppDir that had it and an image that
  dropped it cannot be confused.

What keeps the first one honest is
`TestHelperArtifactsCarryThePinnedThirdPartyNotices` (`internal/helper/deploy/artifacts`,
`-tags helperacceptance`, run by the release workflow's helpers job): it
decompresses every artifact `make helpers` produces and asserts the pinned
document is inside, then runs the host's artifact with `--licenses` and compares
what it prints byte for byte against the pin. A helper built without the notices
— or with a document that is not the pin's — fails there, which is the one place
all four binaries exist to be checked.

**This document does not cover nocx's own Go and npm dependencies**, which is a
separate question with no owner yet; it covers what the pinned archives link,
because that is what ADR-0065 brought into the product.
